title: Instantaneous Velocity
short: The velocity at an instant is the slope of the tangent line to the x–t graph.
trouble: Students think an object at x = 0 must have zero velocity, mixing up position with velocity.

blocks.html: A speedometer shows your velocity right now, not over a trip. On a curved position-time graph the slope keeps changing, so we need the slope at a single point.
The instantaneous velocity at time $t$ is the slope of the tangent line to the $x$–$t$ graph at $t$: the line that just touches the curve there and runs in the same direction.

Take the average velocity over a short interval around $t$, then a shorter one, then shorter still. On a smooth curve, zooming in makes the curve look straighter and straighter, and those average-velocity lines settle down to one line: the tangent. Its slope is the velocity at that instant. In calculus this is the derivative, but the idea only needs slopes.

blocks.title: From a tangent line
blocks.q: The tangent to an $x$–$t$ curve at $t = 2\ \text{s}$ passes through $(1\ \text{s}, 4\ \text{m})$ and $(3\ \text{s}, 8\ \text{m})$. Find the velocity at $t = 2\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: From a short interval
blocks.q: A sensor reads $x = 5.39\ \text{m}$ at $t = 2.9\ \text{s}$ and $x = 5.79\ \text{m}$ at $t = 3.1\ \text{s}$. Estimate the velocity at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.
steps: $v \approx 2.0\ \text{m/s}$. A shorter interval would give an even better estimate.

blocks.html: Thinking an object at $x = 0$ must have zero velocity. Position and velocity are different questions: a car passing the origin at highway speed is at $x = 0$ with a large velocity, and a ball at the top of its rise has zero velocity far from the origin. Check: velocity comes from the slope of the graph, never from its height.
